Interestingly enough, it's a scientifically supported fact that children equate quantity with volume. Allow me to weave two tales to fully explain my perspective, one of my ideal Fallout 4 and one of a "streamlined" Fallout 4:

Part one:

After speaking to a man in the ruins of a small town west of Boston, you learn that a gang of bandits has been raiding the supplies of the locals lately, and the man promises to pay you to get rid of them. You jot down the man's instructions on the location of their hideout in your trusty Pip-Boy, "just south around the hill and in a bunker downriver a ways," he had said. Following his instructions, you eventually reach what seems to be the bunker, but the door to it is securely locked. As you're preparing to take out some lock-picking tools, a man opens a slot in the door and demands a password. You try to persuade him to let you in, but he isn't fooled and you're left outside.

At this point, you have a lot of options, some of which may not have even crossed your mind, but all of which will work with the game's complex mechanics: you could disguise yourself as a bandit and try to gain entry, blast the bunker open with heavy explosives, wait for the bandits to come out on a patrol and sneak in, wait until nightfall and pick the lock on the door, or simply do so now and charge in guns blazing. You feel patient and like doing it smoothly, so you decide to wait for a patrol or raiding party to leave. Besides, your character has spent a lot of time and effort developing stealth related skills and attributes. You make camp in a nearby secluded area and spend some time repairing and maintaining your partially damaged weapons and equipment. Sure enough, a short time later what looks like a raiding party leaves the bunker. After you wait until they're out of sight, you sneak in behind them, knowing that you probably have several hours until they get back.

Thanks to your plan, the bunker on the inside is largely empty, but it has clearly been abandoned for a long time besides the recent occupation of these bandits. You find it easy to get lost in a place like this, as the bunker is large and most of it has clearly never been used by the bandits, but after a short time you hear some voices and follow them to a closed door with a light on the other side. You press your ear to the door to try to hear better; it sounds like there are two or perhaps three men on the other side arguing about something. As you wonder how to proceed, you remember that you have night-vision goggles on your backpack, and that you've noticed the lights in this old bunker flickering since you've arrive. A plan begins to form in your mind and you know how you'll deal with these bandits.

Following what looks like makeshift wiring along the walls which you only just now noticed, you find a generator a few rooms down. Perfect. You put on your night-vision goggles and shut it off, after which you hear cursing from the other direction and a door opening. Now under cover of darkness, you wait behind the door in the generator room for a man to enter. "Piece of shit," he says as he walks into the room and kicks the generator. Turns on he's a ghoul. Before he has a chance to turn it back on, you hit him hard on the back of the head. One down, two to go.

You make your way back to the room where the others are still waiting in the dark. Sure enough, there are two others there, strangely also ghouls. "What the hell is Jefferson doing over there?" one says to the other, and you decide to take this opportunity to finish them off. You pull out your pistol and fire two clean shots into each of their chests, enough in the dark to take them out before they have a chance to react. One dies immediately, but the other lies on the floor coughing up blood. You walk over to finish him off, but he starts to speak. "Wasn't enough to kick us out, huh? To kill our wives and leave the rest to starve? You just had to finish the job, didn't you..." he trails off as he dies. Suddenly you doubt your motivations in coming to exterminate these "bandits," if that's even what they are. Maybe if you had just talked to them instead of shooting first... but you try to put it out of your mind as you head back out; the bunker is clear now.

As you walk back into town, you see the bodies of several ghouls hanging from the old streetlights, recently strung up and already being pecked at by crows. "At least the town defended itself against the raid," you think to yourself as you head back to the man who promised you a reward. "There you are," he says as you walk in. "Hope you cleared out the rest of that subhuman filth; a bunch of them came back this way while you were gone to 'negotiate for food supplies.' Hah, sure showed them." You hesitantly confirm that they won't be "troubling" the town anymore, and head on your way, your purse a bit heavier, but wondering how you might have done things differently.

Part two:

After speaking to a man in the ruins of a small town west of Boston, you learn that a gang of bandits has been raiding the supplies of the locals lately, and the man promises to pay you to get rid of them. A compass marker appears on your screen and you follow it straight to the front door of a bunker, the door of which opens immediately. As you head down the corridor, you encounter several bandits who immediately start shooting at you. You use VATS to score some easy, epic headshots and continue down the path; it's pretty straightforward, no opportunity to get lost.

After you make your way past the lesser bandits and loot them, walk into a room with three men, one of which is labelled "Bandit Leader" by your in-game HUD; you know this'll be a tougher fight. The battle is epic, and after a few grenades thrown at his feet and several dozen bullets fired directly into his body, he finally dies, allowing you to pick up a cool unique gun. Nice. You head back to town and receive a modest reward from the man there, who thanks you for saving the town from those ruthless bandits, in the process giving you enough experience to level up and get a new freely chosen perk before you head on your way.

 

I recognize that this is a ridiculous wall of text, probably the longest I've ever written on Voat, but I hope you'll read it anyway because it illustrates how complexity can substantially improve a game.

I'm not a huge fan of the voiced dialogue. . . but it isn't a deal-breaker or anything. I actually don't see it as taking away options just taking away immersion. I mean, I like to play through as multiple types of characters. Some good, some bad. Some with different backstories for a bit of role-playing. It's easy for me to kind of ignore the story set-up (or even mod it out) with the kid and the wife and everything. But I can't get past the voice. Especially their voice actor. If I want a rough, worn former raider backstory with a gruff, weathered voice their voice actor just won't do! At least with a silent protagonist, I could imagine any voice I wanted, and it actually was very immersive for me. I hope, and imagine people will mod the game to make the protagonist silent. I also am a bit iffy with the skill points. However, I was iffy with Skyrim's simplified leveling system. I think that turned out okay, so I'm confident Bethesda can pull it off in this game as well. I don't see this as a shift to a Bioware audience, even though the dialogue system does seem reminiscent of Mass Effect's dialogue wheel system. The games are still completely different in very key areas. Fallout 4 is still seems to be an open world, go and do really anything just like previous Bethesda RPGs. Mass Effect is very linear, and has very detailed involved story telling. As for the romance options, I don't see anything wrong with the companions being romance-able by either gender. I'd just imagine them as being exclusive to whatever gender I want. I mean, If I want to romance this one girl, I should be able to! I shouldn't have to be one gender or another. It really just opens up more options to either gender to better fit any roleplay background you'd like for each playthrough. I view the romance options as an overall positive change. For an example of the opposite, I look at Dragon Age: Inquisition. I wanted to make my male dwarf character Romance the female elf character. But in the game she is a lesbian. It wouldn't let me! I would have to play through again with a female to romance her. With the way Bethesda is doing it, the romance is really more tailored to the player to let them make their character and their romance interest more varied between playthroughs. I guess it is a way, at least for me, to make my playthrough feel unique from someone else's. Also, I don't think the romancing aspect is to appeal to Bioware RPG fans. It seems that Bethesda had already started to delve into romance with Skyrim (with the marriage system). It looks as if they are simply expanding upon that idea in this game to be a little bit more involved.

Tl;Dr: Iffy about Dialogue system and skills. Romancing is not a big deal. This is not Bethesda appealing to Bioware's audience. Overall I'm not worried about the game being adversely effected.
